name: Conspicuous Consumption
statement: People buy costly, visible luxuries less to use them than to display their wealth and status to others.
statementAccent: to display their wealth and status to others
meaning: Conspicuous consumption is a concept coined by the American economist and sociologist Thorstein Veblen in his 1899 book The Theory of the Leisure Class, referring to the spending of money on, and the acquiring of, luxury goods and services in order to publicly display one's wealth and social status rather than to meet real needs. The point of such consumption is not the usefulness or even the enjoyment of what is bought but the impression it makes on others, signaling economic power and prestige. Veblen developed the idea as part of a satirical critique of the wealthy leisure class, whom he saw as demonstrating their standing through visible waste. Alongside conspicuous consumption he described conspicuous leisure, the display of status through visible idleness and abstention from productive work, and he analyzed pecuniary emulation, the tendency of lower classes to imitate the consumption of those above them. The concept gave rise to the notion of a Veblen good, a good whose demand increases as its price rises, contrary to the normal law of demand, precisely because a higher price signals greater exclusivity and status. Conspicuous consumption became a foundational idea in the sociology and economics of consumption, status, and inequality, and it remains highly relevant to luxury branding and positional goods.
mechanism: Conspicuous consumption works by using visible, costly purchases as signals of social and economic standing. Veblen observed that in a society where wealth confers honor and status, people seek to demonstrate their wealth to others, and the most effective way to do so is through consumption that is visible and manifestly expensive, since the ability to afford waste is proof of pecuniary strength. What is consumed matters less for its practical use than for what it communicates: a luxury good advertises that its owner can command the resources to buy it. This logic drives a dynamic of emulation, in which those lower in the social hierarchy imitate the consumption patterns of those above them in an effort to claim status, prompting the higher ranks to consume ever more conspicuously to maintain their distinction, a competition Veblen linked to invidious comparison. The same logic produces the paradox of the Veblen good, in which raising the price of a luxury item can increase rather than decrease demand, because the higher price enhances the good's power as a status symbol and its exclusivity. Conspicuous leisure follows a parallel logic, displaying status through the visible ability to abstain from productive labor. In all cases, the underlying mechanism is the signaling of relative social position through visible, and often wasteful, expenditure.

examples.text: Purchasing expensive, visible luxuries to display wealth and status rather than to meet a genuine need is conspicuous consumption.
A Veblen good, such as a luxury handbag, can see demand rise as its price rises, because the high price signals exclusivity and status.
Pecuniary emulation drives people to imitate the consumption of those above them, a competition for relative status.

whyItMatters: Conspicuous consumption is a foundational concept in the sociology and economics of consumption, giving lasting expression to the insight that much of what people buy is bought not to use but to signal their wealth and social status to others. Thorstein Veblen's analysis of visible, wasteful expenditure as a display of standing offered a penetrating and satirical critique of consumer culture and the leisure class, and it reframed consumption as a form of social competition rather than mere satisfaction of needs. The concept illuminates status signaling, invidious comparison, and the dynamics of inequality, showing how the pursuit of relative position drives spending and emulation up the social ladder. It gave rise to the influential idea of the Veblen good, which challenges the standard economic law of demand, and it connects to later work on positional goods and the phenomenon of keeping up with the Joneses. Conspicuous consumption remains strikingly relevant to modern luxury branding, marketing, and the study of how status is bought and displayed.

limits: Conspicuous consumption is a powerful concept, but its scope should be understood clearly. Veblen wrote as a critic and satirist of the wealthy leisure class, so the concept carries a normative charge and is a lens on status-driven spending rather than a claim that all consumption is conspicuous, since much consumption meets genuine needs and gives real enjoyment. The Veblen good, whose demand rises with price, is a special and limited case that violates the usual law of demand and applies to particular status goods, not to goods in general, and it should be distinguished from the Giffen good, a different exception. The idea connects to later concepts such as Fred Hirsch's positional goods from 1976, which extend but also refine the analysis.
misreadings: Conspicuous consumption does not claim that all buying is about status; it names the particular kind of visible, wasteful spending aimed at displaying wealth, while much consumption meets real needs. The Veblen good, whose demand rises with price, is a special status-good exception, not a rule about goods in general, and differs from the Giffen good. And Veblen wrote satirically, so the concept is a critique of status display rather than a neutral law, so treating all consumption as conspicuous, the Veblen good as typical, or the idea as value-neutral, misreads Veblen's critical concept.
origin: A concept coined by the American economist and sociologist Thorstein Veblen in his 1899 book The Theory of the Leisure Class, describing the display of wealth and status through visible, wasteful spending on luxury.
